children.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do
children.blurb: In the fall of 2023, nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey took part in a simple test. During math review sessions, some students practiced with a plain AI chat tool, much like the free chatbots anyone can open on a phone.

children.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
children.blurb: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

children.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
children.blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

children.name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
children.blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

sections.body: Getting Oriented is the opening part of the book's treatment of AI in education, and it sets the foundation for everything that comes after. It explains what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool. In this part of school life, AI is not yet being applied to a subject or a task, it is being understood, bounded and prepared for use. The book treats this orientation as the ground on which any later use of AI in a school must stand.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that starting with the foundation works, and it says readers who start nowhere else should start here. What does not work is skipping this ground and moving straight to tools, because the rules set out in these chapters apply to every idea in the chapters that follow. The rule it holds to is that understanding limits, patterns, legal protection and measurement comes before any pilot or purchase. The book also holds that a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool belongs at the start, not as an afterthought.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The four pages fit together as a sequence from capability to pattern to protection to practice. What AI Can and Cannot Do gives the teacher or leader the plain account of the tool's reach and its limits, while Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere gives the recurring ideas that let a reader recognise the same shape across many tools and tasks. Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule is the page a leader or parent would go to for the laws and rules that protect students and for the place of human review, and Pilot, Measure, Scale is the page a teacher or leader would go to for the simple method of trying and judging any new tool before spreading it. Read in that order, the pages move a reader from what the technology is, to what repeats, to what protects, to what to do next.
